common_name: Parksville Beach Woodland Phlox (Pink-Flowered Wild Blue Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in dappled shade, leaving room for the mat to spread into broad colonies over a few seasons.

directions: Parksville Beach is a pink-flowering selection of wild blue phlox discovered as a naturally occurring color variant in the mountains of eastern Tennessee, a striking departure from the blue-violet tones typical of the species. It forms a low, spreading evergreen mat only a couple of inches tall that slowly knits together into broad patches under deciduous shade. In mid-to-late spring it is topped with short clusters of fragrant, bright pink-purple flowers that draw early hummingbirds and native bees. Allow space for the colony to widen, since established plantings spread considerably within a few years.

common_name: Tinian Sprite Woodland Phlox (Compact Pink Wild Blue Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade with good air circulation to limit summer foliage issues.

directions: Tinian Sprite is a compact, pink-flowered selection of woodland phlox that forms a dense low mound well suited to the front of a shaded border or a woodland path edge. Trial evaluations have noted it as a vigorous and consistently floriferous selection, producing an abundant spring display of soft pink blooms over semi-evergreen foliage. Because woodland phlox can be prone to powdery mildew in hot, humid summers, siting it with good air circulation and even soil moisture helps the foliage hold up after flowering. Divide congested clumps in early spring every few years to maintain vigor.

common_name: Blue Ribbons Woodland Phlox (Variegated-Leaf Wild Blue Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, where cooler weather brings out the brightest leaf variegation.

directions: Blue Ribbons is a variegated-foliage selection of wild blue phlox, its leaves marked with cream and soft pink margins that brighten shaded ground even before the spring flowers appear. Clusters of fragrant, lilac-blue flowers open above the foliage in mid-spring, carrying the clove-and-vanilla scent typical of the species. It spreads into a dense, trailing groundcover more vigorously than many straight-species forms, making it useful for covering bare ground beneath trees and shrubs. Give it humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial shade for the best foliage color and bloom.

common_name: Tika Woodland Phlox (Lavender-Flowered Wild Blue Phlox)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial shade, dividing congested clumps every few years to keep the planting vigorous.

directions: Tika is a lavender-flowered selection of wild blue phlox recognized among the named cultivars of the species by university extension plant databases. Like other forms of woodland phlox, it spreads by trailing stems that root at the nodes, gradually forming a loose groundcover beneath deciduous trees. Its early-to-mid spring flowers provide nectar for emerging native bees and butterflies at a time when few other shade perennials are blooming. Plant divisions in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial shade and divide congested clumps every few years.
